bridges.statement: Consciousness belongs to a subject that is not identical to the physical brain or body, establishing a nonphysical human soul.
Mental properties, qualitative experience, and first-person access distinguish consciousness from physical brain states.
Non-degreed personhood and the enduring subject of consciousness require grounding beyond variable physical parts and functions.
Human agents can originate choices for reasons without those reasons causally determining the choices.
Determinism threatens rational warrant because determined belief formation need not track truth-conveying reasons.
How soul and body interact is distinct from whether the soul exists, and their interaction may be a direct primitive action.

bridges.statement: Neither free will nor consciousness supplies sufficient reason to posit a nonphysical human soul.
A choice is either determined by reasons or made without reasons and therefore random, leaving no coherent libertarian alternative.
Brain-dependent predictions and correlations support a material account of consciousness without requiring a soul.
Whether a belief is justified is independent of whether its formation was determined.
A whole can possess properties its component parts lack, so mental and neural property differences do not establish separate substances.
Personhood can be grounded in physical functioning even if its threshold or boundary remains uncertain.
A proposed nonphysical soul needs an assessable interaction with the physical world rather than an unexplained label.
